title: Transient hemiplegia in a patient with migraine: A case of sporadic hemiplegic migraine
case_prompt: A 39-year-old Japanese man with a history of migraine headaches and myofascial pain syndrome was referred for evaluation of transient right-sided hemiplegia. Twenty days earlier, he experienced weakness in his right upper and lower limbs, followed by left occipital pain that resolved with loxoprofen. Two days before presentation, he again developed right upper and lower limb weakness and a tense feeling on the left side of his mouth while at work, and was found unconscious by a colleague. On transport to a local emergency department, he complained of a left occipital headache. Physical examination at that time showed right upper and lower limb muscle weakness and sensory disturbance on the ulnar side of the right upper arm. Noncontrast head CT and MRI showed no edema, infarction, hemorrhage, or acute lesions. Laboratory testing revealed normal blood counts and chemistries. His symptoms gradually improved, and he was discharged to outpatient referral when the etiology remained unclear. On first visit to our hospital, his temperature was 36.6°C, blood pressure 139/91 mmHg, and pulse 70/min. He reported a mild left parietal headache and fatigue. Current medications included lomerizine hydrochloride, diazepam, meloxicam, and a Japanese herbal medicine. On examination, cranial nerves, motor strength, and sensation were normal except for decreased pain sensation in the left frontal region. No skin lesions or muscle atrophy were noted. Blood tests were unremarkable, and electroencephalography showed no epileptiform activity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stroke or transient ischemic attack was considered given the acute hemiplegia, but was excluded because “Noncontrast head CT and MRI ... showed no edema, infarction, hemorrhage, or acute lesions.”  
2. Epilepsy was considered, but a detailed history differentiated convulsive seizures from aura because “a detailed history can be used to distinguish convulsive seizures (sudden, usually <1 min) from HM aura (progressive, >20 min).”  
3. Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome was included in the broad differential diagnosis, as noted: “The differential diagnoses for HM are broad and include … reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome ….”  
4. Carotid artery dissection was considered, as noted: “The differential diagnoses for HM are broad and include … carotid artery dissection ….”  
5. Meningitis or encephalitis was considered, as noted: “The differential diagnoses for HM are broad and include … meningitis/encephalitis ….”  
6. Intracranial tumors were considered, as noted: “The differential diagnoses for HM are broad and include … tumors ….”  
7. Hysteria was considered, as noted: “The differential diagnoses for HM are broad and include … hysteria.”  
8. Cerebral hemorrhage was distinguished based on headache timing because “Headaches associated with cerebral hemorrhage develop abruptly, whereas HM typically progresses gradually with aura symptoms.”  
9. Transient ischemic attack was further distinguished from migraine aura by pattern and duration because “TIAs present with acute onset motor or sensory deficits ... with symptoms subsiding within minutes to an hour ... In contrast, migraines involve sequential symptom development, beginning with visual disturbances … lasting for 20–30 min or longer … migraines typically include headaches following neurological symptoms.”
